events.text:
This is game 77 in a series of 9×9 Go games. Each new game starts in a fresh session.

## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If CLAUDE.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session; your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

Your working directory holds:
- CLAUDE.md (113,931 bytes)
- count.py (828 bytes)
- libs.py (1,378 bytes)

## This game

A new game. You play Black, so you move first.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: your Read, Write, Edit, Glob and Grep tools, for any file in your working directory.

You also have a shell, and you may write and run code in it; Python is available as `python3`. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.

Trying to race against White's bottom chain doesn't help either since they hold three liberties to my two. Looking further, the top chain and the F4-F6 chain both have more liberties than I can threaten quickly, so capturing anything nearby to rescue my group seems unlikely to work in time.

Working through the C6/B6/C5 sequences, every variation I try leaves my center group with too few liberties — White keeps connecting C4 with B5 or C5, pushing my own group to zero new liberties. It looks like this center group is effectively dead unless there's some ladder tactic I'm missing, so I'm checking a B4 atari line to see if it changes the outcome.

If instead White plays B6 after my C6, I'm forced to C5, but that move gains nothing for my liberties while leaving White's C4 stone in atari — still a losing race overall.

Given this, the central group looks dead unless I find a way to get compensation elsewhere. Losing six stones is a huge setback, so I'm considering whether attacking the F-chain or bottom chain first could create enough counter-pressure, even though White could still cash in on my center group while I'm maneuvering.

This group really does look dead unless White misplays, so I should focus on practical compensation instead of trying to save it. White still has to spend a move to actually capture, so maybe I can use that tempo to grab value elsewhere, like cutting off the bottom chain by playing F3 and seeing how White responds before committing further.

C4 doesn't seem capturable by ladder since White escapes via C5 and puts me in atari, so my center looks dead and White's top chain is too healthy to attack with 5 liberties. I'm trying to find any forcing sequence — F3 only pressures the bottom chain to 2 libs without helping my center, and C6 reduces my own group to 2 libs without a clear follow-up threat.

I need to accept the center is likely lost and think about what's salvageable: F3 might provoke a local response from White saving the bottom chain, which could at least open up some capturing potential if that chain's liberties get exposed.

Running through the race scenarios for the bottom group versus center, it looks like White wins every version — defending the bottom group costs me too much locally. Given that, I'm leaning toward playing elsewhere for maximum points, like enclosing the right side, and letting White spend a move on the capture instead.

Still, F3 seems to do double duty — cutting off White's bottom from the main chain while claiming territory on the right. Checking liberties if White ataris at F2, I'd extend to G3, which keeps the group alive and adds liberties.

Alternatively, G4 feels like a solid hane but likely doesn't give me enough to win the overall position.

I'll gamble on F3 since a weaker opponent might mishandle the tactical fight, even though a 2-liberty stone normally violates good shape principles.
